scenes.label: Establish the path
scenes.text: Start with four endpoints and one optical circuit switch. The controller selects a connection from endpoint A to endpoint B. Inside the switch, the optical signal follows that established path. The switch does not need to read each packet to decide where the signal goes.

scenes.label: Locate packet services
scenes.text: The electrical endpoints still generate and receive traffic. Packet inspection, buffering, and quality of service can exist in those surrounding systems. They are not functions supplied by the transparent optical path itself.

scenes.label: Introduce competing demand
scenes.text: Now endpoint C also needs to communicate with B. The optical switch does not magically combine two independent demands onto the same dedicated connection. The broader system must decide how to allocate its available connectivity and when to change it.

scenes.label: Separate setup from transfer
scenes.text: This gives us two distinct activities: selecting a circuit, then transferring data through it. Bufferless operation removes packet queuing inside the optical switch. It does not promise that an entire network is free of contention. Keep that boundary in mind whenever you evaluate an OCS benefit.

scenes.label: Long stable phase
scenes.text: A switching time becomes meaningful only when we compare it with the workload. Consider a cluster whose connections stay useful for a long communication phase. A relatively slow reconfiguration may be acceptable when the system can establish the circuits before that phase begins.

scenes.label: Frequent change
scenes.text: Now consider a different workload that needs new connections much more frequently. If reconfiguration consumes most of the available interval, the useful transfer window shrinks. The same switching mechanism can therefore be a good fit for one workload and a poor fit for another.

scenes.label: Select the mechanism
scenes.text: Robotic patching, mirror steering, polarization control, material deformation, on-chip routing, and phase steering provide different design options. Their actual timing depends on the implementation. Even within silicon photonics, electro-optic and thermo-optic actuation have different speed and power characteristics.

scenes.label: Balance constraints
scenes.text: Do not stop at the fastest number. Check the required port count, the end-to-end optical loss budget, the power used to change and maintain a state, and the maturity of the design. The best physical fit is the one that satisfies these constraints within the workload’s available switching window.

scenes.label: Read the starting fabric
scenes.text: Begin with this simplified fabric. Electrical packet switches connect groups of endpoints through an electrical interconnect stage. Following one optical link through that stage requires optical-to-electrical conversion, packet processing, and conversion back to light.

scenes.label: Identify the changed layer
scenes.text: Now identify the layer that an optical circuit switching architecture changes. We replace the selected interconnect stage with a fabric of configurable optical paths. This is an architectural example, not a port-for-port drawing of a particular production network.

scenes.label: Retain endpoint functions
scenes.text: The surrounding electrical switches remain important. They still handle packet functions while the optical fabric provides selected connectivity between them. A controller can revise those connections as the deployment requires. This does not mean that every endpoint has a permanently dedicated path to every other endpoint.

scenes.label: Consider an upgrade
scenes.text: Finally, consider an endpoint speed upgrade. The optical switching path does not interpret the bit rate, so it can avoid the electronic switching limits of the replaced stage. Engineers must still verify transceiver compatibility, optical bandwidth, insertion loss, and the complete link budget. Rate transparency is a valuable property, not a waiver of system engineering.

scenes.label: Distinguish three layers
scenes.text: ACTINA and OCS-BCube explore how optical connectivity can adapt to training workloads. Keep three things separate as you read this conceptual illustration: the physical connections that are available, the traffic that the workload needs to send, and the control decisions that allocate optical capacity. This is a research architecture, not a claim of a deployed production system.

scenes.label: Observe the current demand
scenes.text: During one iteration, some communicating groups need more bandwidth than others. A traffic-aware controller uses that demand to choose an allocation supported by the architecture. In the source concept, wavelength-reconfigurable transceivers are part of the mechanism that changes this allocation.

scenes.label: Reconfigure at the boundary
scenes.text: At the next iteration boundary, the demand changes. The controller revises the wavelength assignments and connectivity allocation. The physical topology still constrains which paths are possible; changing a wavelength does not create an arbitrary new fiber connection.

scenes.label: Use the revised allocation
scenes.text: The following communication phase uses the revised allocation. The teaching point is the relationship between demand, control, and available optical paths. Performance depends on prediction, reconfiguration overhead, the transceiver design, and the workload. Research results must retain their evaluation conditions rather than become universal production promises.

scenes.label: Expose capabilities
scenes.text: An optical component becomes useful in a deployed system only when the surrounding ecosystem can understand and control it. Start with a technology supplier. The supplier describes the supported ports, optical behavior, and operating limits of the device.

scenes.label: Integrate control
scenes.text: A systems integrator connects those capabilities to orchestration software. The software needs an unambiguous way to describe a requested circuit and to interpret the state that the device reports. Shared data models help both sides attach the same meaning to that information.

scenes.label: Operate and verify
scenes.text: An operator requests a connection and checks that the resulting physical state matches the intended service. Hardware capability, software control, and operational evidence must all agree. A working optical component alone does not establish interoperability across an entire system.

scenes.label: Improve the shared contract
scenes.text: Open specifications, reference architectures, and validation work make these handoffs easier to repeat across organizations. Experience from suppliers, integrators, operators, and researchers can then inform the next revision. This is an illustrative workflow, not a particular published OCP interface. The practical opportunity is to contribute clear requirements and evidence at the handoff your team understands best.
